title: The kitchen rota (Rule 35)
hookLine: everyone takes a turn serving in the kitchen, even the abbot

cards: Who's cooking tonight? Benedict answers that question for his whole monastery in a single chapter. The brothers, he says, are to serve one another.
Nobody is let off kitchen duty. The only exceptions are the sick, and a brother busy with something more pressing for the house. Everyone else takes a week.

Scholar, singer, the one who copies books, the one who hoes the beans: each in turn puts on the apron and feeds the others, and then, at the week's end, cleans up and hands the job on. A rota, in the plain old sense.
A list on the wall, and your name comes round.

teach.b: Benedict gives two reasons, and neither is efficiency. First, he says, serving this way earns a greater reward. Second, it builds love.
Not love as a feeling. Love as a habit of the hands, learned by carrying plates to people you didn't choose. Paul put it plainly: "by love serve one another."
Now look how kind the chapter is. The weak, Benedict says, should get helpers, so nobody serves in misery.
The cooks for the week get a little extra bread and drink beforehand, so they can serve without grumbling and without going hungry. He knows exactly how hungry people get while feeding others.
Then the handover, on the last day of the week. The outgoing servers wash the towels. They hand back the pots and pans to the cellarer, clean and in one piece.
And the servers going off and the servers coming on wash the feet of everyone in the house. Feet, after a week of serving food.
It's hard not to hear Jesus here, at the last supper, a towel tied around him: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet."

Then, in chapel, the cook going off duty thanks God for help and comfort, and the one coming on asks for help, with a psalm verse said three times, which the King James gives as: "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD."
Even the dishes start with a prayer for help.

how: In Benedictine houses, monks and nuns take turns at serving meals and kitchen work, often by the week, and the handover is marked with prayer in chapel as the Rule describes.

games.q: you're the abbot drawing up the kitchen list. your best scholar asks to be let off so he can keep writing. what does the Rule say?
o: let him off. his work matters more.
only the sick, or someone on more urgent business, is excused.

games.why: nobody is let off kitchen service except for sickness, or work of greater need for the house. serving builds love.

practice: Picture the kitchen you'll be in today, at home, at work, wherever food happens, and the person who usually does the serving and clearing there; see their face.

Choose one job that's usually theirs, the dishes, the coffee, the table, the trash, and decide to take it, with no announcement. If you pray, say the psalm line before you start: make haste to help me.

wordCard.voice: The kitchen rota. Benedict's weekly turns of serving, so that nobody is only ever served and love becomes a habit of the hands.
